stem: What does an entity-relationship diagram show?

options.content: The entities and their relationships
options.rationale: Correct: with the degree of each relationship.

options.content: The order in which a program runs
options.rationale: That is a flowchart.

options.content: The network cables joining computers
options.rationale: That is a network diagram.

options.content: The sequence of stages in a project
options.rationale: That is a project plan.

explanation: An E-R diagram models the entities and relationships of a database.

stem: In crow's foot notation, what does the three-pronged end of a line mean?

options.content: Many
options.rationale: Correct: the 'foot' marks the many end of a relationship.

options.content: One
options.rationale: A single bar marks the one end.

options.content: Optional
options.rationale: A small circle marks an optional end.

options.content: Primary key
options.rationale: Keys are not shown by the end of a line.

explanation: The crow's foot is drawn at the many end of a relationship.

stem: Why can a many-to-many relationship not be stored directly in a relational database?

options.content: Primary keys cannot be unique in such a relationship
options.rationale: Primary keys can still be unique.

options.content: One foreign key field can hold only one value, not many
options.rationale: Correct: a link table is needed.

options.content: SQL does not allow two tables to be joined together by a key
options.rationale: SQL can join tables.

options.content: The data would be impossible to sort
options.rationale: Sorting is not the reason.

explanation: A foreign key holds a single value, so the relationship is split with a link table.

stem: A shop records customers and the orders they place. One customer places many orders and each order is placed by one customer. Which relationship is this?

options.content: One-to-one
options.rationale: A customer can have more than one order.

options.content: One-to-many
options.rationale: Correct: one customer, many orders.

options.content: Many-to-many
options.rationale: Each order has only one customer.

options.content: No relationship
options.rationale: Orders are placed by customers, so the tables are related.

explanation: One customer has many orders and each order has one customer, so it is one-to-many.

stem: A shop records customers and the orders they place. One customer places many orders and each order is placed by one customer. In which table is the foreign key placed?

options.content: `Customer`, holding the order's primary key
options.rationale: That would allow only one order for each customer.

options.content: Neither, because a link table is always needed
options.rationale: A link table is only needed for many-to-many relationships.

options.content: `Order`, holding the customer's primary key
options.rationale: Correct: the many side holds the foreign key.

options.content: Both tables, each holding the other's primary key
options.rationale: One foreign key is enough.

explanation: The foreign key goes on the many side: the Order table holds CustomerID.
hints: Which table has many records for each record of the other?

stem: A school database records which teachers teach which classes. A teacher teaches many classes and a class has many teachers. Which design is correct?

options.content: A `ClassID` field in the `Teacher` table holding every class
options.rationale: One field cannot hold several classes.

options.content: A `TeacherID` field in the `Class` table holding every teacher
options.rationale: One field cannot hold several teachers.

options.content: A single table that repeats every field in both entities
options.rationale: That causes redundancy.

options.content: A link table holding a foreign key to each of the two tables
options.rationale: Correct: it splits the many-to-many relationship.

explanation: A many-to-many relationship needs a link table with two foreign keys.
hints: How many teachers does each class have?

stem: A designer stores `Forename Surname` together in one field called `Name`. Which design principle is broken, and why does it matter?

options.content: Every table needs a foreign key; the table cannot be linked
options.rationale: Not every table needs a foreign key.

options.content: Primary keys must be text; the key cannot be sorted
options.rationale: Primary keys are not required to be text.

options.content: Attributes should be atomic; surname searches would be hard
options.rationale: Correct: each field should hold one value.

options.content: Fields must be calculated; the value may be out of date
options.rationale: Calculated values should not be stored, but the name is not calculated.

explanation: Separate fields for forename and surname make sorting and searching by surname possible.
hints: How would you sort by surname?

stem: A database for a football league has the entities `Team`, `Player` and `Match`. A team plays many matches and a match involves two teams. Which statement about the relationship between `Team` and `Match` is correct?

options.content: It is one-to-many, with the foreign key `MatchID` in `Team`
options.rationale: A team plays many matches, so one MatchID in Team is not enough.

options.content: It is one-to-one, because each match has one result
options.rationale: The result of a match is a different matter.

options.content: It does not need a relationship because the matches are shown in the results
options.rationale: Stored matches must be linked to the teams that played them.

options.content: It is many-to-many, so a link table such as `Fixture` is needed
options.rationale: Correct: each team plays many matches and each match has two teams.

explanation: Team and Match are many-to-many; a link table resolves it.
hints: How many matches does a team play, and how many teams are in a match?

stem: The foreign key of a one-to-many relationship is placed in the table on the 'one' side.
explanation: False. It goes on the many side and holds the primary key of the one side.

stem: A link table that resolves a many-to-many relationship contains foreign keys to both of the original tables.
explanation: True. It turns the relationship into two one-to-many relationships.

stem: A person's age should be stored in a table instead of the date of birth, because it is quicker to read.
explanation: False. Age changes every year, so the stored value goes out of date. Store the date of birth and calculate the age.
hints: Does a person's age stay the same?

stem: Match each design step to what is done in it.

right.content: Add a link table with two foreign keys
Decide the primary key of each table and place the foreign keys
List each table with its fields and keys
List the things about which data must be stored
List the properties of each entity

explanation: These steps are applied in order to move from a scenario to tables.

stem: A vet records `Owner` and `Pet`. An owner may have many pets and each pet has one owner. Complete the design.

payload.template: The relationship is {{blank:a}}. The foreign key {{blank:b}} is placed in the {{blank:c}} table.

explanation: One owner has many pets, so Pet holds the OwnerID foreign key.
hints: Which table is on the many side?

stem: Name the table that is added to resolve a many-to-many relationship.
explanation: A link table (also called a junction or associative table) splits the relationship in two.

stem: A hostel database holds `Student` and `Room`. A student may rent a room in different terms and a room is rented by many students over time. What is the name of the type of table that must be added to store which student has which room? (one or two words)
explanation: A link table (for example Tenancy) stores the StudentID and RoomID.
hints: Which kind of table splits a many-to-many relationship?

stem: A youth club has 18 members. Each member takes part in exactly 3 of the club's activities. A link table `Participation` stores one row for each member and activity pair. How many rows does the table hold?
hints: One row is stored for each pairing of a member with an activity.

stem: A bus company has the entities Driver, Bus and Route. Each driver drives many buses over time and each bus is driven by many drivers. Each bus runs on one route, and a route has many buses. After the many-to-many relationship is resolved, how many tables are needed in total?
explanation: Three entity tables and one link table.
workedSolution:
1. Entity tables: Driver, Bus, Route = 3.
2. Driver and Bus are many-to-many, so one link table is added = 1.
3. Total = 4.
hints: Count the entity tables, then the link tables.

stem: Explain why a link table is needed to store a many-to-many relationship. [3]

points.description: A relational database cannot store a many-to-many relationship directly, because a foreign key field can hold only one value
The link table holds a foreign key to each of the two tables
This turns the relationship into two one-to-many relationships

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A foreign key can hold only one value, so a many-to-many relationship cannot be stored directly. The link table holds a foreign key to each of the two tables, which turns the relationship into two one-to-many relationships.

explanation: Foreign key limit, two foreign keys, two one-to-many relationships.
hints: Say what the problem is, then what the link table holds.

stem: A library records books, the authors who wrote them and the members who borrow them. Identify three entities that the database must hold and give one attribute for each. [3]

points.description: Book with an attribute such as Title or ISBN
Author with an attribute such as Name
Member with an attribute such as Name or Phone (Loan is also an acceptable entity)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Book (Title), Author (Name) and Member (Phone).

explanation: Entities are the nouns about which data is stored.
hints: Look for the nouns in the description.

stem: A designer proposes that the `Member` table stores `Age` and `FullName`. Suggest two improvements to the design and give a reason for each. [4]

points.description: Store date of birth instead of age
Age changes every year and would go out of date; it can be calculated from the date of birth
Split FullName into Forename and Surname
Each attribute should hold one value so that searches and sorting by surname work

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Store the date of birth instead of age, because age goes out of date and can be calculated. Split the full name into forename and surname, because each field should hold a single value so that sorting and searching by surname are possible.

explanation: Avoid stored calculated values and non-atomic fields.
hints: Consider each of the two attributes in turn.

stem: A letting agent in Harare records Blocks of flats, Flats and Tenants. Each block contains many flats and each flat is in one block. A tenant may rent several flats over the years and a flat has several tenants over the years.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the type of relationship between `Block` and `Flat`.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: State the type of relationship between `Flat` and `Tenant`.
parts.explanation: Many tenants over the years; many flats over the years.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: In which table is the foreign key `BlockID` placed?
parts.explanation: Flat is on the many side.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Describe how the relationship in part (b) is stored in the database.

points.description: A link table such as Tenancy is added
It has a foreign key FlatID and a foreign key TenantID
It may also hold the start and end dates of the tenancy, and the primary key is a new identifier or the combination of keys and start date

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A link table, Tenancy, is added with the foreign keys FlatID and TenantID, and the start and end dates of the tenancy.

parts.explanation: The link table splits the relationship.

explanation: Each flat has one block and each block has many flats; the pairs are Block-Flat and Flat-Tenancy.
hints: A tenant rents one flat at a time but over the years a flat has many tenants.

stem: A netball club in Kariba has Teams, Players and Coaches. Each coach looks after one team, and a team has one coach. A player may play for different teams in different seasons, and a team has many players in a season.

parts.label: (a)
parts.explanation: Each coach looks after one team and each team has one coach.

parts.label: (b)
parts.explanation: Players play for many teams over time; teams have many players.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Describe the design of the table that resolves the relationship in part (b). Name the table and its fields.

points.description: A link table such as Squad is added
It contains the foreign keys PlayerID and TeamID
A Season field (or similar) is included so that the same player and team can be recorded in different seasons; the key includes it

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Squad(PlayerID, TeamID, Season). PlayerID and TeamID are foreign keys and the primary key is the three fields together.

parts.explanation: Link table with the two foreign keys and the season.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Write the relational schema for the three entity tables, marking the primary keys and foreign keys.

points.description: Coach with CoachID as primary key
Player with PlayerID as primary key
Team with TeamID as primary key and CoachID as a foreign key (or Coach holding TeamID)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Coach(CoachID, Name); Player(PlayerID, Name, DateOfBirth); Team(TeamID, TeamName, CoachID) where CoachID is a foreign key.

parts.explanation: Each table has an identifier; the one-to-one link needs one foreign key.

explanation: Entities Coach, Player, Team; players join many teams over time and a team has many players, so a link table is needed.
